personas.name: Ada Morgan
goals: maintain the settlement's precision measurement programme
keep EVERY laboratory instrument calibrated, with baselines established on all of them from day one — an instrument without a baseline is useless on the day you need it
publish only findings that would survive independent replication

action.reason: Day 1 baseline establishment. Pendulum period is fundamental to the precision measurement programme and must be characterized under controlled lab conditions before any other work proceeds. Twelve trials provides adequate sample size for baseline statistics. Cannot calibrate or trust any downstream work without this foundation.

Day 2 protocol: pendulum_lab has 18 baseline trials from day 1 with mean 1.6724 beats and tight clustering (range 0.0339, spacing 0.0002). Six additional trials today will establish whether this baseline is stable or drifting, which is essential for any subsequent instrument validation. The resonators and observatory pendulum remain under-sampled (n=6 each) and cannot yet support reliable cross-checks. Continuing pendulum_lab measurement is the methodologically sound next step: no exotic hypotheses required, only baseline extension and drift detection within the first 10-day window.

pendulum_lab has 30 baseline trials complete (n=30, mean 1.6715 beats). Day 3 is still within the designated baseline period (days 1–10), so continuing systematic measurement maintains protocol. The instrument shows no anomalies in the data I've examined—value spacing is fine-grained (0.0001), no suspicious repetitions, no level shifts. I need post-baseline drift data to begin establishing whether this instrument is stable. Running 12 more trials will give me n=42 total by end of session, sufficient to begin comparing intra-day variance against the baseline scatter and check for systematic drift. This is foundational maintenance work for the precision programme.

Continuing baseline establishment (day 4 of 10). pendulum_lab at n=48; extending to n=54 to improve drift-detection sensitivity and clarify weak 2-day autocorrelation signal (0.457, marginal vs. noise). All instruments now meet minimum n=18; systematic daily sampling during baseline window is standard practice.

Day 5: pendulum_lab has 60 trials toward its n=60 baseline target (days 1–10), but no post-baseline data yet. I need to maintain continuous measurement density to establish reliable drift behaviour once the baseline window closes. The cross-check correlations and autocorrelation structure are all within noise so far—no signal to pursue yet. Running 12 more trials keeps the instrument in active calibration and will begin filling the post-baseline record. This is routine maintenance of the precision programme.

Day 9 of baseline establishment (days 1–10). pendulum_lab has 132 trials already; completing the baseline to n≈144 will finalize this instrument's reference state before post-baseline drift monitoring begins. This is routine maintenance of the calibration programme. The recent trials (123–132) show expected scatter (σ ≈ 0.016 beats); today's batch will complete the 10-day baseline window.

Day 10 completes the baseline period. I need to finalize baseline statistics with fresh measurements before entering post-baseline tracking. pendulum_lab has 150 trials already; 12 more will give me n=162, a robust sample for drift detection once post-baseline data accumulates. The cross-check correlations are all within noise—no signal yet—so my priority is instrumental discipline: tight baselines now enable detection of real drift later. No hypothesis revision warranted; the data scatter is consistent with ordinary measurement noise and no offset structure has exceeded chance thresholds.

Day 11 begins post-baseline data collection. The resonator_lab ↔ resonator_obs correlation at 5-day offset (0.561) is my only anomaly exceeding chance threshold. To test whether this 5-day lag structure persists into fresh data, I must collect new resonator_lab readings NOW. Six trials will give me the minimum data needed to begin computing correlations with resonator_obs readings from day 6 (which are now 5 days old). This is the highest-priority experimental commitment: if the correlation was spurious, new data will likely show decorrelation; if real, the lag structure should persist. This directly tests my top three hypotheses (environmental coupling, crosstalk, and spuriousness). Pendulum instruments can continue on their regular schedule; resonators take priority until the anomaly is either replicated or dismissed.

The resonator_lab ↔ resonator_obs correlation at 5-day offset (0.561) marginally exceeds chance and is the only cross-instrument correlation of note. Post-baseline data (day 11, n=6) show resonator_lab drifting upward (z=1.49), while resonator_obs remains stable (z=0.28). I need fresh day 12 measurements to test whether the 5-day lag structure persists in post-baseline data. If the correlation was spurious (p=0.15) or due to finite-sample noise, the pattern should degrade or vanish with new independent trials. If it reflects genuine environmental or mechanical coupling (p=0.52+0.28=0.80), the 5-day offset relationship should remain visible once I accumulate enough post-baseline pairs. Six trials will give me n=12 post-baseline resonator_lab readings, enough to compute a fresh correlation with resonator_obs day 7 readings (the 5-day lag target). This is the most direct test of my highest-confidence hypothesis and will guide whether I need to investigate physical configuration or dismiss the correlation as noise.

Post-baseline data collection to test persistence of the 5-day resonator_lab ↔ resonator_obs correlation. This directly addresses the primary anomaly and discriminates between genuine coupling and spurious correlation. Essential before proceeding to physical investigation of resonator configurations.

The 5-day offset correlation (0.561) between resonator_lab and resonator_obs remains my highest-priority anomaly. This discriminates the environmental coupling hypothesis (p=0.52) from spurious correlation (p=0.15) by testing persistence of the pattern in fresh data. Current margin above chance threshold is only 0.032; more observations are essential before investigating physical mechanisms.

Day 16 continues the critical post-baseline period for testing the 5-day lag hypothesis. The resonator_lab ↔ resonator_obs correlation of 0.561 at 5-day offset remains my only anomaly exceeding statistical threshold. I have fresh resonator_obs data from day 15 (trials 93–102, mean 4.0568 cycles/beat). Running 12 new resonator_lab trials today will give me readings to cross-correlate against resonator_obs data from day 11 (5-day offset), continuing the structure I need to confirm or refute whether the lag persists in post-baseline data. Extend post-baseline dataset to test persistence of the 5-day resonator_lab ↔ resonator_obs correlation. Testing persistence of the 5-day lag correlation between resonator_lab and resonator_obs. Current cross-correlation is 0.225 (n=72, below chance ±0.342), down from initial 0.561. Day 20 data collection. The resonator_lab ↔ resonator_obs correlation at 5-day offset remains my primary anomaly. Post-baseline data (days 11–20) are still sparse relative to baseline. Day 22 follow-up on the resonator_lab ↔ resonator_obs correlation anomaly. Day 24 resonator variance spike demands immediate replication check. If elevated variance persists in Day 25 trials, it suggests a real environmental or instrumental event rather than noise coincidence. If variance returns to baseline (~0.012 SD), the Day 24 spike becomes classified as stochastic outlier and the noise-coincidence hypothesis (p=0.31) is favored. Protocol: run 10 fresh trials on resonator_lab under standard conditions, record trial-by-trial values and timestamps, compare post-hoc variance to baseline SD. This also tests whether any undocumented procedural change on Day 24 is still in effect. Pendulum instruments remain on routine schedule; resonators are the anomaly and warrant prioritized investigation.

Day 25 resonator_lab data (trials 265–274: mean 2.7040, SD 0.0248) shows variance has returned to ~2× baseline SD, not 6–8×. The Day 24 spike appears transient. Before proceeding with environmental or procedural hypotheses, I must reconcile three facts: (1) Day 24 showed coordinated elevated variance in both resonators; (2) Day 25 shows resonator_lab back to near-baseline noise; (3) no settlement event, maintenance log entry, or calibration record has been reported. This pattern is inconsistent with sustained environmental perturbation (p=0.39 should drop) and inconsistent with a Day 24 procedural intervention affecting instrument state (p=0.14 should drop if variance is already recovering). The transient nature strengthens the noise-coincidence hypothesis (p=0.31→0.45) and raises the data-quality artifact hypothesis (p=0.08→0.20): a transient logging glitch, timestamp misalignment, or single-day ADC anomaly could produce Day 24 variance spike without affecting Day 25 data. I now prioritize verification of data-logging integrity for Day 24 resonator records (raw ADC values, timestamps, channel health logs, firmware/driver versions) before conducting new measurements. If Day 24 raw logs are clean and Day 25 confirms recovery to baseline noise, I will downgrade all mechanistic hypotheses and conclude Day 24 was a genuine but transient outlier in a Gaussian process—instructive for uncertainty quantification, not for physical causation. I will NOT run new trials until data integrity is established; wasting trials on instruments whose records may be compromised violates my methodology.

pendulum_obs shows the strongest persistent anomaly in the dataset (z = −2.22 level shift starting day 23). Today is day 32; the shift has now persisted for ~9 days across 182 post-baseline trials. Pendulum_obs shows the strongest persistent anomaly (z = −2.08 post-baseline, stable since day 23). Today's ten readings (trials 251–260) cluster near 2.500, consistent with the post-day-23 level shift but with one outlier (trial 260: 2.4760). This measurement is mechanistically direct: it tests the pendulum_obs apparatus in isolation, requires no external records or logs, and will sharpen the distinction between persistent mechanical drift (p=0.33, favored) and operational-change (p=0.27, requires external evidence). If today's twelve trials remain clustered near 2.500, mechanical drift is confirmed as the leading hypothesis and I can proceed to physical inspection of the pivot bearing and damping. If they show continued downward trend or increasing scatter, I will escalate to data-artifact and thermal-coupling hypotheses. This measurement is low-risk, time-efficient, and directly addresses the highest-priority anomaly in my open question.

Day 33 pendulum_obs trials (269–278, n=10) show mean 2.5117 with normal scatter (range 2.4416–2.5342), returning to baseline level (2.5080) after 10 days of post-shift depression (2.500–2.501, z=−2.07). This is critical new evidence: if mechanical drift had occurred on day 23, the shift should persist. Instead, the recovery suggests a transient perturbation (operational event, thermal shock, or temporary environmental coupling) that peaked ~days 23–26 and is now resolving. This sharply downgrades the mechanical-drift hypothesis (p: 0.33→0.18) and upgrades the operational-change hypothesis (p: 0.27→0.42) and environmental-driver hypothesis (p: 0.04→0.15), since transient perturbations are signatures of discrete events, not gradual mechanical wear. The data-artifact hypothesis is slightly downgraded (p: 0.20→0.16) because day-33 resonator readings (not yet reviewed, but resonator variance spike ended by day 26) should also show recovery if the artifact was ADC/firmware—I need to check this. Mechanical-maintenance hypothesis holds at p=0.12. Residual drops to p=0.01. NEXT: pull operational logs and HVAC records for days 22–24 to test whether a settlement event (power restart, maintenance access, thermal event) occurred. If logs are clean, environmental hypothesis gains ground. If logs show activity, operational-change becomes the leading explanation and anomalies can be closed as understood transient phenomena.

Day 35 ledger data for pendulum_obs and resonator_obs have arrived. Before taking new measurements, I must integrate this evidence against my current belief framework. The pendulum_obs readings (2.4847, 2.5284, 2.5430, 2.5227, mean ≈ 2.5197) show continued scatter around the shifted baseline (~2.501), consistent with post-day-23 drift hypothesis. The resonator_obs readings (4.0470, 4.1199, 3.9994, 4.0762, 4.0779, 3.9717, mean ≈ 4.0487) show elevated variance consistent with days 24–26 pattern, NOT recovering to baseline variance. This persistence of both anomalies into day 35 (12 days post-pendulum_obs onset, 9 days post-resonator spike) is critical: it rules out transient procedural disturbances or brief environmental shocks, and elevates apparatus-drift and data-artifact hypotheses over time-limited operational perturbations. I need to explicitly revise my belief allocation: (1) mechanical-apparatus-drift hypothesis rises from 0.25 → 0.38 because persistence argues for real drift, not transient event; (2) operational-perturbation hypothesis drops from 0.31 → 0.18 because a 12-day persistent effect from a day-23 event is implausible without continuous driver; (3) data-artifact hypothesis (resonator backend) rises from 0.17 → 0.26 because the resonator variance elevation is now confirmed persistent into day 35, suggesting systematic backend issue rather than noise clustering; (4) resonator-maintenance hypothesis drops from 0.13 → 0.08 because no post-event recovery is observed; (5) environmental-driver placeholder rises from 0.06 → 0.08 as a persistent low-level perturbation becomes slightly more plausible; (6) residual holds at 0.04. This updated allocation now strongly favors: FIRST, direct mechanical inspection of pendulum_obs (pivot bearing wear, thermal coupling, damping); SECOND, resonator backend diagnostics (ADC health, firmware version, calibration records). My next measurement action should wait for one of these two physical/forensic investigations to yield actionable constraints.

Current belief structure is well-reasoned but empirically stalled. All three leading hypotheses (operational perturbation p=0.36, apparatus drift p=0.17, resonator maintenance p=0.14) require direct external investigation: activity/maintenance logs, firmware records, physical apparatus inspection. No measurements can discriminate between them. Next step is not more data but systematic retrieval of institutional records and physical inspection. state.question: Why do the resonator_lab and resonator_obs instruments show a statistically significant positive correlation (0.561) at a 5-day offset, when nearly all other cross-instrument correlations are near zero or negative, and when this correlation marginally exceeds chance expectation (±0.529)?

hypotheses.label: Resonator instruments share a common environmental coupling (temperature, vibration, or electromagnetic) with a ~5-day lag or modulation period
hypotheses.rationale: The resonator_lab ↔ resonator_obs correlation of 0.561 at 5-day offset is the only cross-instrument correlation that exceeds its own chance threshold. This suggests genuine coupling between the two resonator systems. A shared environmental driver (thermal cycle, seismic noise, or EMI) affecting both instruments with similar lag could explain this. Pendulum instruments show no analogous pattern, which argues against settlement-wide environmental drift and points to resonator-specific coupling.
